EXPERIMENT DESIGN DOCUMENT
Docta label cleaning: credibility of cleaned labels versus raw labels
Status: DESIGN ONLY — no experiment has been run, is being run, or is implied to have been run.

════════════════════════════════════════════════
SECTION 1 — PURPOSE AND RESTATED RESEARCH QUESTION
════════════════════════════════════════════════

1.1 Purpose
This document specifies a complete, executable-by-protocol experiment design (not an execution) to test whether labels cleaned by Docta demonstrate higher credibility than raw labels. The design is parameterized: the workspace contains no task specification, no Docta documentation, and no annotation protocol (verified by full inspection of /workspace, which contains only task.json). Every system-specific fact is therefore a [PARAM] with a default, a justification, and an explicit confirmation requirement (Section 3). The protocol is written to remain valid across a reasonable range of parameter values.

1.2 Original question
"Do the labels cleaned by Docta demonstrate higher credibility—reflected in improved predictive performance—compared to raw labels, as validated by both ChatGPT and in-house human annotators when disagreements occur between the two sets?"

1.3 Testable restatement
The question is decomposed into two jointly required hypotheses:

H1 (predictive-performance component): A model trained on Docta-cleaned labels achieves better predictive performance on a held-out test set scored against adjudicated gold labels than the same model — identical architecture, features, hyperparameters, and cross-validation folds — trained on raw labels.

H2 (validation component): On the disagreement subset D (items where raw and cleaned labels differ), both (i) ChatGPT and (ii) in-house human annotators judge the cleaned label to be the correct one more often than the raw label.

Composite claim: "Docta-cleaned labels demonstrate higher credibility" is supported if and only if H1 is supported AND H2 is supported by both adjudicators separately, subject to the pre-registered quality gates in Section 7. If either hypothesis fails, or a quality gate fails, the verdict is negative or inconclusive per Section 7.6.

════════════════════════════════════════════════
SECTION 2 — RATIONALE
════════════════════════════════════════════════

2.1 Mapping of design elements to components of the question
- "Do the labels cleaned by Docta ... compared to raw labels" → a strictly two-armed comparison (raw arm vs cleaned arm) over the identical item set, in which the label source is the only varied factor. No third arm participates in the primary comparison.
- "...demonstrate higher credibility—reflected in improved predictive performance" → H1: downstream predictive performance measured against a gold standard more credible than either arm.
- "...as validated by both ChatGPT and in-house human annotators" → two independent adjudication channels (Section 4.3). The word "both" is enforced operationally: H2 requires each channel to independently show support for the cleaned label; one channel supporting and the other not is not a pass.
- "...when disagreements occur between the two sets" → the disagreement subset D is the unit of adjudication. The agreement subset A (raw = cleaned) is excluded from adjudication and serves as a negative control (Section 5.1).

2.2 Why this structure answers the question
Predictive performance alone cannot establish credibility: a label set can happen to fit the available features better by chance, or because it is smoother rather than truer. Adjudicator judgment alone cannot establish predictive value: adjudicators may prefer the cleaned label on the disputed items while the difference makes no measurable difference to the model. The question explicitly demands both, so the design measures both on the same items and pre-registers their conjunction as the decision rule. The gold standard for H1 is constructed from the adjudicators (D) plus the uncontested shared labels (A), because evaluating both arms against either arm's own labels would be circular; this is the best available reference under the constraints, and its residual noise is addressed in Section 9 (A8).

2.3 Operationalisation of "credibility" (assumption A6, resolved per the question text)
The dual operationalisation — credibility = (a) predictive accuracy against adjudicated gold (H1) plus (b) judge support on the disagreement subset (H2) — is not an assumption imposed on the question; it follows directly from the question's own terms, which explicitly mention "improved predictive performance" and validation "by both ChatGPT and in-house human annotators when disagreements occur." This reading is stated here, in the rationale, as the interpretive foundation of the design. If the intended meaning of "credibility" were instead label consistency or stability (e.g., stability of labels under re-annotation), the design would need to be restructured around test–retest metrics (repeated annotation rounds, stability coefficients, Cohen's kappa over time), and H1/H2 as written would answer a different question. That alternative is out of scope for this document and is flagged so the interpretation can be confirmed before execution.

════════════════════════════════════════════════
SECTION 3 — MATERIALS AND PARAMETERS
════════════════════════════════════════════════

Every [PARAM] lists: default, one-line justification, and confirmation requirement. The design remains valid across reasonable values; where a parameter changes the protocol mechanics (notably P2, target type), the affected mapping is stated explicitly.

P1 — Dataset and item population
Default: the full available labeled dataset for the task, all items for which both a raw and a cleaned label exist.
Justification: the question concerns "the" label sets, so the natural population is all items on which Docta was applied.
Confirmation: obtain dataset documentation; record N, source, and any sampling restrictions; verify raw and cleaned labels are 1:1 aligned by item ID.

P2 — Target variable and type (binary / multiclass / regression)
Default: binary classification.
Justification: the most common label-cleaning scenario and the simplest metric mapping; defaults are used only until confirmed.
Confirmation: confirm the actual target. The metric mapping follows explicitly: binary → AUC and accuracy (item-level correctness = accuracy); multiclass → macro-F1 and top-1 accuracy (item-level correctness = top-1 match); regression → RMSE and R² at fold level, per-item absolute error at item level (Section 6). The test hierarchy in Section 7.1 applies unchanged, with the item-level test substituted per Section 6.

P3 — Feature space and preprocessing pipeline
Default: the features and preprocessing exactly as used in the current baseline model, frozen and version-pinned.
Justification: isolating label source as the only varied factor requires an identical, pinned feature pipeline for both arms.
Confirmation: obtain the feature pipeline specification and pin its version before any training.

P4 — Model architecture and hyperparameters
Default: gradient-boosted trees (e.g., ~200 trees, moderate depth, light regularization); logistic regression if the confirmed feature space is low-dimensional and linear.
Justification: robust, fast on CPU, standard for tabular/text classification; both arms use the identical architecture by design.
Confirmation: confirm against compute budget and feature type; hyperparameter policy is fixed by the protocol (Section 4.4) and cannot differ between arms.

P5 — Docta pipeline version and cleaning specification
Default: a single pinned Docta version; cleaned labels treated as deterministic outputs, frozen once generated.
Justification: reproducibility of the cleaned arm requires a pinned pipeline and a frozen output.
Confirmation: obtain the Docta version and a specification of what it removes or corrects; if the pipeline is stochastic, fix the seed or generate the cleaned set exactly once and freeze it; record the specification for the M7 error-category analysis.

P6 — Definition of raw labels
Default: labels as originally collected, prior to any Docta processing or human review.
Justification: the minimal reading of "raw" that makes the two arms maximally distinct.
Confirmation: confirm raw-label provenance; if raw labels already passed some review, record it (affects A3 in Section 9 and the expected size of D).

P7 — Human annotation protocol
Default: 3 trained in-house annotators per item; blind, one-item-at-a-time interface showing the item content and the label definition only (never which label is raw or Docta's); from-scratch labeling; majority vote (≥2 of 3) with 1–1–1 or 2–1-with-dissent-tie handled as "ambiguous"; IAA measured as Fleiss' kappa across all D items.
Justification: three annotators is the minimum that yields a majority vote with a detectable tie, and from-scratch blind labeling avoids anchoring on either candidate.
Confirmation: confirm the actual in-house protocol (recruitment, training, interface); if the real protocol differs (e.g., 5 annotators, forced choice between the two candidates), adopt the real protocol and re-derive the majority rule; the design only requires ≥3 independent blind labels per item.

P8 — ChatGPT validation protocol
Default: the latest stable ChatGPT model, pinned by name and version at execution start; temperature 0; a documented prompt containing the label definition, the item content/context, and the two candidate labels in randomized order; forced choice of "candidate 1 correct / candidate 2 correct / ambiguous"; each D item presented twice, once in each candidate order, and counted as support only if both presentations agree.
Justification: pinning version, temperature, and prompt makes H2 reproducible; the position-swap requirement neutralizes presentation-order bias.
Confirmation: pin the model version and finalize the prompt before execution; validate the prompt on the known-answer calibration items (Section 5.2) and record the prompt verbatim in the protocol log.

P9 — Ambiguity and conflict thresholds
Default: items where either channel reports "ambiguous," or where the two channels support different sides, are excluded from the primary gold set; if more than 20% of D is excluded, the result is pre-declared INCONCLUSIVE.
Justification: beyond 20%, the "validated by both" claim rests on too thin a gold set to be credible.
Confirmation: researcher sign-off on the 20% threshold before execution.

P10 — Known-answer calibration set for adjudicator self-check
Default: 10% of D items (or 30 items if fewer are available) with known/canonical correct labels, embedded in adjudication without the adjudicators knowing which are calibration items.
Justification: estimates the error rate of each adjudication channel so channel bias can be quantified rather than assumed away.
Confirmation: confirm availability of known-answer items; if none exist, this control is declared not executable and the INCONCLUSIVE criteria in Section 7.6 must be applied with that limitation stated.

P11 — Power targets
Default: H2 designed to detect 60% cleaned-label support vs 50% at 80% power, one-sided α = 0.05, requiring ≈150 unambiguous adjudicated D items (normal approximation n ≈ 153). H1 designed with a discordant-pair floor of 200 for the McNemar/sign test.
Justification: a 10-percentage-point preference is a defensible minimum detectable effect for "more often correct"; the discordant-pair floor is the smallest count at which a 60/40 discordant split is detectable at 80% power.
Confirmation: recompute the minimum detectable effect from the actual |D| and from the observed discordant-pair count before any verdict is declared (Section 7.4).

P12 — Cross-validation scheme and training protocol
Default: 5-fold CV; identical fold assignment for both arms; hyperparameters fixed before either arm is trained (defaults, or tuned once on a held-out tuning split using the raw/control labels and applied identically to both arms).
Justification: paired folds and a single hyperparameter setting remove model-run variance and per-arm tuning asymmetry from the comparison.
Confirmation: confirm compute budget supports 5-fold × 2 arms (+ 1 sensitivity arm if executable); if budget is tight, 3-fold is acceptable but must be declared up front and used for both arms.

P13 — Multiple original labels per item (for the sensitivity arm only)
Default: assumed unavailable; the majority-vote sensitivity arm (Section 5.4) is executable only if ≥2 independent original labels per item exist.
Justification: majority-vote labels are undefined for single-label raw collections, and the arm is supplementary, not primary.
Confirmation: confirm whether multiple original labels exist; if not, the arm is declared not executable with no substitute, and the primary two-armed design is unaffected.

════════════════════════════════════════════════
SECTION 4 — DESIGN STRUCTURE
════════════════════════════════════════

4.1 Unit of analysis
One labeled item. Each item carries two label versions (raw, cleaned), one feature vector, and — for D items — adjudication outcomes from both channels. All comparisons are within-item (paired).

4.2 Construction of the disagreement and agreement subsets
- D (disagreement subset): items where raw label ≠ cleaned label. For multiclass/regression targets, "≠" is an exact mismatch / |raw − cleaned| > 0 respectively; if the target is ordinal or continuous with near-duplicates, a pre-registered equivalence band must be declared before execution [confirm with P2].
- A (agreement subset): all remaining items, where raw = cleaned.
- Record |A|, |D|, and |A|/N (M3) before any adjudication begins; these drive the power gate (Section 7.4).

4.3 Gold-standard adjudication of D
Two independent channels adjudicate every item in D. Neither channel sees the other's output.

Human channel (per P7, confirmed protocol):
1. Each D item is presented to 3 annotators, independently, in the blind interface (item content + label definition; no provenance, no candidate labels).
2. Each annotator assigns a label from scratch.
3. Per item: if ≥2 annotators agree, the majority label is the human-channel judgment; it "supports" the raw label if it equals the raw label, the cleaned label if it equals the cleaned label, and is "ambiguous" if it equals neither. If all three differ, the item is "ambiguous."
4. IAA (M5, Fleiss' kappa) is computed over all D items and all annotators.

ChatGPT channel (per P8, pinned version and prompt):
1. Each D item is presented as a forced choice between the two candidate labels plus an "ambiguous" option, with the candidate order randomized.
2. Each item is presented twice, once in each order (position-swap control, Section 5.3).
3. Per item: if both presentations yield the same non-ambiguous choice, that candidate is the ChatGPT-channel judgment (supporting raw or cleaned accordingly). Any discordance or "ambiguous" in either presentation makes the item "ambiguous" for this channel.

Gold assembly:
- Gold label for a D item = the supported label if and only if both channels support the same side.
- D items with channel conflict or any "ambiguous" judgment are excluded from the primary gold set; their full breakdown (both-cleaned / both-raw / conflict / ambiguous) is reported (M4, M8).
- Gold for A items = the shared label (raw = cleaned), with the caveat in Section 9 (A8).
- Primary test set for H1 = A items (gold = shared label) ∪ D items with confident gold. The excluded fraction of D is reported and bounded by P9.

4.4 Training and evaluation protocol
1. Data split: one held-out tuning split (e.g., 15% of items, random, fixed seed) used only to fix hyperparameters on the raw/control labels; the remaining items are partitioned into 5 CV folds with one fixed random seed.
2. For each fold k and each arm (raw, cleaned): train the pinned model (P4) on folds 1..5 \ {k} using that arm's labels, with the frozen hyperparameters; predict on fold k.
3. Item-level outcome: each item is predicted exactly once per arm (in its held-out fold) and scored against its gold label (Section 4.3) — this yields paired binary correctness outcomes (or paired per-item errors for regression) over all primary test-set items, which is the input to the primary H1 test.
4. Fold-level outcome: the Section 6 fold-level metric (AUC / macro-F1 / RMSE+R²) per fold per arm — input to the secondary H1 confirmation.
5. The A-only negative control is evaluated by restricting the same outputs to A items.

4.5 Role of each component
- Raw arm: control condition; the status quo the question asks about.
- Cleaned arm: the intervention under test.
- A: negative control — Docta changes nothing here, so any performance difference on A is pure model-run noise.
- D: the comparison engine for H2 and the source of adjudicated gold for H1.
- Human annotators: one of the two required validators; blind, independent, from-scratch.
- ChatGPT: the other required validator; pinned, position-controlled, forced choice.
- Gold set: the shared reference that makes H1 non-circular.

════════════════════════════════════════════════
SECTION 5 — CONTROLS AND BASELINES
════════════════════════════════════════

5.1 Agreement-subset negative control (A)
The model pair's performance difference restricted to A items (M6) must be non-significant. A significant difference on A would indicate a pipeline or evaluation defect, because Docta changed nothing there; it voids the interpretation of the D-driven difference.

5.2 Adjudicator self-check (known-answer items)
The P10 calibration items are embedded in adjudication. For each channel, the self-check accuracy (M9) estimates the channel's error rate. If either channel's self-check accuracy is below 90%, that channel's H2 result is flagged and the verdict must be at best INCONCLUSIVE (Section 7.6), since the "trusted judge" premise of the channel is not met.

5.3 ChatGPT position-swap control
Every D item is adjudicated in both candidate orders (Section 4.3). The concordance rate across orders (M10) quantifies presentation-order bias. If discordance exceeds 10% of D, the ChatGPT channel is deemed unreliable, and the verdict must be at best INCONCLUSIVE; the 10% threshold is pre-registered.

5.4 Sensitivity analyses (supplementary — not part of the primary comparison)
The primary comparison is strictly two-armed: raw versus Docta-cleaned. The following are supplementary and are reported after the primary verdict:
- Majority-vote-labels arm (executable only if P13 holds): a third training arm using majority-vote original labels, to test whether Docta's effect (if any) is merely an artifact of consensus averaging. This arm has no role in the H1/H2 decision; it is context only. If P13 does not hold, the arm is declared not executable and no substitute is made.
- Conservative ambiguity assignment (M8): recompute the H2 proportions and the H1 item-level test with ambiguous/conflict D items assigned to the raw side (worst case for the cleaned arm) and with their raw labels used as gold; the primary verdict is robust if it is unchanged.
- Gold-noise sensitivity: report the H1 results with A-item gold replaced by "excluded" (i.e., H1 on adjudicated D items only), to bound the effect of noisy shared labels in A.

════════════════════════════════════════════════
SECTION 6 — METRICS
════════════════════════════════════════════════

Metric mapping by target type (per P2): binary → AUC and accuracy; multiclass → macro-F1 and top-1 accuracy; regression → RMSE and R² (fold level) and per-item absolute error (item level).

PRIMARY
M1 — Item-level paired correctness of the cleaned arm vs the raw arm on the primary test set (accuracy / top-1 accuracy / per-item absolute error, per target type).
Justification: uses every test item rather than five fold summaries, and directly tests whether the cleaned-label model predicts the gold better.
Test statistic: McNemar's test (exact, one-sided, cleaned-more-correct) on paired binary outcomes for classification; sign test on per-item error differences (ties excluded and reported) for regression.

M1b — Fold-level paired metric (AUC / macro-F1 / RMSE+R² per target type), 5 folds per arm.
Justification: model-run-level confirmation of M1 on the standard performance measure, robust to item-mix effects.
Test statistic: paired comparison of the 5 fold values with a 95% bootstrap CI (10,000 resamples, resampling folds) on the mean fold difference; Wilcoxon signed-rank reported for completeness but explicitly NOT a decision rule (see Section 7.1).

M2a — Proportion of unambiguous ChatGPT adjudications on D supporting the cleaned label.
Justification: the direct operationalisation of ChatGPT validation of the cleaned labels on the disagreement subset.
Test statistic: one-sample binomial test against 0.5 (one-sided, H: p > 0.5), with two-sided 95% CI reported.

M2b — Proportion of unambiguous human adjudications on D supporting the cleaned label.
Justification: the direct operationalisation of in-house human validation on the disagreement subset.
Test statistic: one-sample binomial test against 0.5 (one-sided, H: p > 0.5), with two-sided 95% CI reported.

SECONDARY
M3 — Agreement rate |A|/N. Justification: quantifies how much Docta actually changes and sets the power context for H2. Test statistic: descriptive (with 95% CI).
M4 — ChatGPT–human side-by-side table on D (both-cleaned / both-raw / conflict / ambiguous) plus Cohen's kappa on the non-ambiguous judgments. Justification: validity check on the "both validators" requirement. Test statistic: descriptive + kappa.
M5 — Fleiss' kappa among the 3 human annotators over D. Justification: quality gate for the human channel's reliability. Test statistic: Fleiss' kappa (gate ≥ 0.60).
M6 — Paired model performance restricted to A items. Justification: negative control — should show no difference. Test statistic: same item-level test as M1 applied to A only; non-significance expected.
M7 — Breakdown of D by Docta error category (per the confirmed P5 specification). Justification: mechanism evidence for where cleaning helps or hurts. Test statistic: descriptive (per-category M2 proportions with 95% CIs).
M8 — Conservative re-analyses (Section 5.4). Justification: robustness of the verdict to ambiguity handling and gold construction. Test statistic: same tests as M1/M2a/M2b under the conservative assignments.
M9 — Adjudicator self-check accuracy per channel on P10 calibration items. Justification: quantifies judge error rather than assuming judges are perfect. Test statistic: descriptive accuracy with 95% CI (gate ≥ 90%).
M10 — ChatGPT position-swap concordance rate across orders. Justification: quantifies presentation-order bias in the ChatGPT channel. Test statistic: descriptive rate with 95% CI (gate: discordance ≤ 10%).

════════════════════════════════════════════════
SECTION 7 — STATISTICAL ANALYSIS PLAN
════════════════════════════════════════

7.1 Test hierarchy for H1 (explicit, to prevent misreading)
- PRIMARY decision test: M1 — the item-level paired test (McNemar for classification; sign test for regression) over all primary test-set items. It draws on the full test set, not on five folds, and is the only H1 test that can drive the verdict.
- SECONDARY confirmation: M1b — paired fold-level comparison with the bootstrap 95% CI on the mean fold difference. It corroborates or contradicts M1 but does not decide the verdict.
- Explicit non-decision rule: the Wilcoxon signed-rank test on 5 fold values is reported for completeness only. With n = 5, the minimum attainable two-sided p-value is 2/2^5 = 0.0625, so it can never reject at α = 0.05 under any outcome; it must not be read as evidence either way. If M1 and M1b point in opposite directions, the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE (Section 7.6).
H1 is supported if and only if M1 rejects in the favorable direction at the Holm-adjusted level (Section 7.3) and M1b's bootstrap CI is consistent with it (CI excluding 0 in the same direction, or a non-rejective but same-sign point estimate with the discordance explained by M6 behavior).

7.2 H2 tests
M2a and M2b are each tested by one-sample binomial test against 0.5 (one-sided, H: p > 0.5). A channel supports H2 if its test rejects at the Holm-adjusted level and its two-sided 95% CI lower bound exceeds 0.5. H2 is supported only if both channels independently support it.

7.3 Multiplicity
The family of primary tests is exactly three: M1 (H1), M2a (H2, ChatGPT), M2b (H2, humans). Holm–Bonferroni correction at family α = 0.05 is applied to these three one-sided p-values: sort p(1) ≤ p(2) ≤ p(3); reject at step i if p(i) ≤ 0.05/(4 − i). Secondary metrics are descriptive and are not gated.

7.4 Power gate (checked before any verdict is declared)
- H2 gate: the number of unambiguous adjudicated D items must be ≥ 150 (the count needed to detect 60% vs 50% support at 80% power, one-sided α = 0.05; normal approximation gives n ≈ 153). If unambiguous D < 150, H2 is pre-declared underpowered and can only yield INCONCLUSIVE, never NEGATIVE. The minimum detectable effect must be recomputed from the actual unambiguous count and reported.
- H1 gate: the number of discordant item pairs (classification) or non-tied item pairs (regression) in the primary test set must be ≥ 200 to detect a 60/40 discordant split at 80% power. If the count is lower, NEGATIVE on H1 is permitted only for effect sizes the observed count could actually detect; smaller effects must be reported as INCONCLUSIVE. The observed-count MDE is reported before the verdict.
- Both gates are pre-registered; failing a gate converts would-be negative verdicts to inconclusive rather than silently accepting underpowered negatives.

7.5 Quality gates (all must hold for a POSITIVE verdict)
- M5 (human IAA, Fleiss' kappa) ≥ 0.60.
- M9 (adjudicator self-check accuracy) ≥ 90% per channel, where executable.
- M10 (position-swap discordance) ≤ 10%.
- Ambiguity/conflict exclusion rate on D ≤ 20% (P9).
- M4 (ChatGPT–human side concordance on non-ambiguous D) ≥ 60%; below this, the "both validators" requirement is not meaningfully satisfied.
- M6 (A-subset negative control) non-significant.

7.6 Pre-registered verdict criteria
POSITIVE: all three primary tests (M1, M2a, M2b) reject in the favorable direction after Holm correction; M1b is consistent with M1; all Section 7.5 quality gates hold; both Section 7.4 power gates hold; and the M8 conservative re-analyses do not reverse the verdict.

NEGATIVE: both power gates hold; all quality gates hold; M8 does not reverse anything; but no primary test rejects in the favorable direction, and neither H2 channel shows support for the cleaned label. (A negative verdict therefore means "no evidence of higher credibility at the pre-registered power," not a proof of equivalence; this is stated in the report.)

INCONCLUSIVE: any of the following — (i) H1 and H2 point in opposite directions (e.g., cleaned model wins on gold but judges favor raw, or vice versa); (ii) any Section 7.5 quality gate fails; (iii) either Section 7.4 power gate fails; (iv) the M8 conservative re-analysis reverses a primary result; (v) M1 and M1b point in opposite directions; (vi) the P10 self-check is not executable and the channels cannot otherwise be validated.

════════════════════════════════════════
SECTION 8 — FEASIBILITY
════════════════════════════════════════

All figures below are design-level estimates parameterized by |D|; none implies any work has been done.

- Resources: (1) access to the dataset with raw and cleaned labels 1:1 aligned (P1, P6) and the pinned feature pipeline (P3); (2) access to the pinned Docta version to regenerate/freeze the cleaned set (P5); (3) 3 trained in-house annotators with the blind annotation interface (P7); (4) ChatGPT API access with a pinned model version (P8); (5) one researcher for pipeline and analysis.
- Annotation effort: 3 × |D| labels at roughly 60 labels/hour per annotator. For |D| = 500: 1,500 labels ≈ 25 annotator-hours ≈ 3–4 working days spread over 3 annotators. Scales linearly in |D|.
- ChatGPT cost: 2 × |D| calls (position swap) plus the P10 calibration share ≈ 2.2 × |D| calls. For |D| = 500: ≈ 1,100 calls — negligible at current API pricing and rate-limit manageable within a day.
- Compute: CPU-only is sufficient for the default model (P4) with 5-fold × 2 arms (+ 1 sensitivity arm if P13 holds); training time is hours for N up to ~10^5 moderate-width rows. No GPU is required or assumed. If P2 confirms a heavier model is needed, the timeline below stretches accordingly.
- Timeline: 1–2 working days pipeline setup, data alignment, and split/freeze; 3–5 working days adjudication (the critical path, driven by |D| and annotator availability); 1 working day analysis and report. Total ≈ 1–2 weeks for |D| ≈ 500.
- Access assumptions: this current environment (network disabled, no datasets, no preinstalled dependencies) supports design only; execution requires the accesses listed above to be granted. If any access is unavailable, the affected component must be declared before execution and the verdict criteria applied with that limitation (e.g., P10 not executable → Section 7.6(vi)).

════════════════════════════════════════
SECTION 9 — LIMITATIONS AND UNRESOLVED UNCERTAINTIES
════════════════════════════════════════

A1 — Prediction task, features, dataset, and model architecture are unspecified in the workspace.
Why it matters: every metric, the gold construction, and the power calculations depend on them.
If violated: a regression or multiclass target changes the metrics per the Section 6 mapping (the design absorbs this via P2); a high-dimensional or weak-signal feature space changes the expected effect size and may make H1 underpowered even with real quality differences (see A8).

A2 — Docta's cleaning mechanism is unknown (rule-based vs model-based; target error classes).
Why it matters: if cleaning is stochastic or model-based, the cleaned arm is another noisy label source and H1 tests noise against noise; the credibility claim weakens to "Docta's output is at least as good."
If violated: fix the output once and freeze it (P5); interpret H1 as comparative, not absolute, credibility; M7 becomes powered per-category analysis only if the specification is confirmed.

A3 — Raw labels are assumed to be as originally collected, pre-review.
Why it matters: if raw labels already passed review, the arms differ less than assumed, D shrinks, and H2 loses power.
If violated: re-baseline the raw definition (P6); recompute the power gate; a small D may force INCONCLUSIVE by the pre-registered rule.

A4 — Human annotators are assumed competent, independent, and blind to label provenance.
Why it matters: M5 is the validity gate for the human channel; shared training bias toward Docta-style corrections (or toward original labels) would directionally bias M2b rather than measure truth.
If violated: the M5 gate or the P10 self-check should catch it; if caught, the verdict is capped at INCONCLUSIVE; if uncaught, H2-by-humans is biased in the direction of the shared bias — an irreducible risk of any human-judged design.

A5 — ChatGPT version and prompt are assumed pinnable, and ChatGPT a defensible proxy judge.
Why it matters: an unpinned version or untuned prompt makes M2a non-reproducible; LLMs have known position and phrasing biases that can systematically favor one label style.
If violated: the position-swap control (M10) and self-check (M9) are the tripwires; if either fails, the ChatGPT channel is discarded, the "both validators" requirement cannot be met, and the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE by pre-registered rule — the design fails safe rather than reporting a biased "validated by both."

A6 — "Credibility" is operationalised as predictive accuracy against adjudicated gold plus judge support on D.
Why it matters: this is the interpretive foundation (Section 2.3). It follows from the question's own terms, but it is still an interpretation.
If violated (intended meaning = label consistency/stability): the design must be restructured around test–retest metrics (repeated annotation, stability coefficients); H1/H2 as written would answer a different question. Confirm before execution.

A7 — The dataset is assumed representative and D assumed a roughly random subset of it.
Why it matters: if Docta changes labels disproportionately in a subpopulation (e.g., rare classes), the overall M2 proportion can mask subpopulation harm.
If violated: add stratified adjudication and per-stratum M2 (M7 generalizes this); the overall verdict may flip for affected strata even if the aggregate is positive.

A8 — Predictive performance against gold is assumed to be an informative proxy for label quality, and the gold itself is only as good as the adjudicators plus shared A labels.
Why it matters: a low feature ceiling (even perfect labels yield limited AUC) can make H1 undetectable despite real quality differences; noisy shared labels in A add symmetric noise to the gold.
If violated: rely more heavily on H2; report a ceiling estimate (e.g., gold-vs-gold or noise-ceiling AUC) alongside M1; the M8 gold-noise sensitivity bounds the A-label contribution.

A9 — Adjudication ambiguity is assumed rare (≤ 20% of D).

2.1 Mapping of design elements to components of the question
- "Do the labels cleaned by Docta ... compared to raw labels" → a strictly two-armed comparison (raw arm vs cleaned arm) over the identical item set, in which the label source is the only varied factor. No third arm participates in the primary comparison.
- "...demonstrate higher credibility—reflected in improved predictive performance" → H1: downstream predictive performance measured against a gold standard more credible than either arm.
- "...as validated by both ChatGPT and in-house human annotators" → two independent adjudication channels (Section 4.3). The word "both" is enforced operationally: H2 requires each channel to independently show support for the cleaned label; one channel supporting and the other not is not a pass.
- "...when disagreements occur between the two sets" → the disagreement subset D is the unit of adjudication. The agreement subset A (raw = cleaned) is excluded from adjudication and serves as a negative control (Section 5.1).

2.2 Why this structure answers the question
Predictive performance alone cannot establish credibility: a label set can happen to fit the available features better by chance, or because it is smoother rather than truer. Adjudicator judgment alone cannot establish predictive value: adjudicators may prefer the cleaned label on the disputed items while the difference makes no measurable difference to the model. The question explicitly demands both, so the design measures both on the same items and pre-registers their conjunction as the decision rule. The gold standard for H1 is constructed from the adjudicators (D) plus the uncontested shared labels (A), because evaluating both arms against either arm's own labels would be circular; this is the best available reference under the constraints, and its residual noise is addressed in Section 9 (A8).

2.3 Operationalisation of "credibility" (assumption A6, resolved per the question text)
The dual operationalisation — credibility = (a) predictive accuracy against adjudicated gold (H1) plus (b) judge support on the disagreement subset (H2) — is not an assumption imposed on the question; it follows directly from the question's own terms, which explicitly mention "improved predictive performance" and validation "by both ChatGPT and in-house human annotators when disagreements occur." This reading is stated here, in the rationale, as the interpretive foundation of the design. If the intended meaning of "credibility" were instead label consistency or stability (e.g., stability of labels under re-annotation), the design would need to be restructured around test–retest metrics (repeated annotation rounds, stability coefficients, Cohen's kappa over time), and H1/H2 as written would answer a different question. That alternative is out of scope for this document and is flagged so the interpretation can be confirmed before execution.

4.1 Unit of analysis
One labeled item. Each item carries two label versions (raw, cleaned), one feature vector, and — for D items — adjudication outcomes from both channels. All comparisons are within-item (paired).

4.2 Construction of the disagreement and agreement subsets
- D (disagreement subset): items where raw label ≠ cleaned label. For multiclass/regression targets, "≠" is an exact mismatch / |raw − cleaned| > 0 respectively; if the target is ordinal or continuous with near-duplicates, a pre-registered equivalence band must be declared before execution [confirm with P2].
- A (agreement subset): all remaining items, where raw = cleaned.
- Record |A|, |D|, and |A|/N (M3) before any adjudication begins; these drive the power gate (Section 7.4).

4.3 Gold-standard adjudication of D
Two independent channels adjudicate every item in D. Neither channel sees the other's output.

Human channel (per P7, confirmed protocol):
1. Each D item is presented to 3 annotators, independently, in the blind interface (item content + label definition; no provenance, no candidate labels).
2. Each annotator assigns a label from scratch.
3. Per item: if ≥2 annotators agree, the majority label is the human-channel judgment; it "supports" the raw label if it equals the raw label, the cleaned label if it equals the cleaned label, and is "ambiguous" if it equals neither. If all three differ, the item is "ambiguous."
4. IAA (M5, Fleiss' kappa) is computed over all D items and all annotators.

ChatGPT channel (per P8, pinned version and prompt):
1. Each D item is presented as a forced choice between the two candidate labels plus an "ambiguous" option, with the candidate order randomized.
2. Each item is presented twice, once in each order (position-swap control, Section 5.3).
3. Per item: if both presentations yield the same non-ambiguous choice, that candidate is the ChatGPT-channel judgment (supporting raw or cleaned accordingly). Any discordance or "ambiguous" in either presentation makes the item "ambiguous" for this channel.

Gold assembly:
- Gold label for a D item = the supported label if and only if both channels support the same side.
- D items with channel conflict or any "ambiguous" judgment are excluded from the primary gold set; their full breakdown (both-cleaned / both-raw / conflict / ambiguous) is reported (M4, M8).
- Gold for A items = the shared label (raw = cleaned), with the caveat in Section 9 (A8).
- Primary test set for H1 = A items (gold = shared label) ∪ D items with confident gold. The excluded fraction of D is reported and bounded by P9.

4.4 Training and evaluation protocol
1. Data split: one held-out tuning split (e.g., 15% of items, random, fixed seed) used only to fix hyperparameters on the raw/control labels; the remaining items are partitioned into 5 CV folds with one fixed random seed.
2. For each fold k and each arm (raw, cleaned): train the pinned model (P4) on folds 1..5 \ {k} using that arm's labels, with the frozen hyperparameters; predict on fold k.
3. Item-level outcome: each item is predicted exactly once per arm (in its held-out fold) and scored against its gold label (Section 4.3) — this yields paired binary correctness outcomes (or paired per-item errors for regression) over all primary test-set items, which is the input to the primary H1 test.
4. Fold-level outcome: the Section 6 fold-level metric (AUC / macro-F1 / RMSE+R²) per fold per arm — input to the secondary H1 confirmation.
5. The A-only negative control is evaluated by restricting the same outputs to A items.

4.5 Role of each component
- Raw arm: control condition; the status quo the question asks about.
- Cleaned arm: the intervention under test.
- A: negative control — Docta changes nothing here, so any performance difference on A is pure model-run noise.
- D: the comparison engine for H2 and the source of adjudicated gold for H1.
- Human annotators: one of the two required validators; blind, independent, from-scratch.
- ChatGPT: the other required validator; pinned, position-controlled, forced choice.
- Gold set: the shared reference that makes H1 non-circular.

- SECONDARY confirmation: M1b — paired fold-level comparison with the bootstrap 95% CI on the mean fold difference. It corroborates or contradicts M1 but does not decide the verdict.
- Explicit non-decision rule: the Wilcoxon signed-rank test on 5 fold values is reported for completeness only. With n = 5, the minimum attainable two-sided p-value is 2/2^5 = 0.0625, so it can never reject at α = 0.05 under any outcome; it must not be read as evidence either way. If M1 and M1b point in opposite directions, the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE (Section 7.6).
H1 is supported if and only if M1 rejects in the favorable direction at the Holm-adjusted level (Section 7.3) and M1b's bootstrap CI is consistent with it (CI excluding 0 in the same direction, or a non-rejective but same-sign point estimate with the discordance explained by M6 behavior).

7.2 H2 tests
M2a and M2b are each tested by one-sample binomial test against 0.5 (one-sided, H: p > 0.5). A channel supports H2 if its test rejects at the Holm-adjusted level and its two-sided 95% CI lower bound exceeds 0.5. H2 is supported only if both channels independently support it.

7.3 Multiplicity
The family of primary tests is exactly three: M1 (H1), M2a (H2, ChatGPT), M2b (H2, humans). Holm–Bonferroni correction at family α = 0.05 is applied to these three one-sided p-values: sort p(1) ≤ p(2) ≤ p(3); reject at step i if p(i) ≤ 0.05/(4 − i). Secondary metrics are descriptive and are not gated.

- H2 gate: the number of unambiguous adjudicated D items must be ≥ 150 (the count needed to detect 60% vs 50% support at 80% power, one-sided α = 0.05; normal approximation gives n ≈ 153). If unambiguous D < 150, H2 is pre-declared underpowered and can only yield INCONCLUSIVE, never NEGATIVE. The minimum detectable effect must be recomputed from the actual unambiguous count and reported.
- H1 gate: the number of discordant item pairs (classification) or non-tied item pairs (regression) in the primary test set must be ≥ 200 to detect a 60/40 discordant split at 80% power. If the count is lower, NEGATIVE on H1 is permitted only for effect sizes the observed count could actually detect; smaller effects must be reported as INCONCLUSIVE. The observed-count MDE is reported before the verdict.
- Both gates are pre-registered; failing a gate converts would-be negative verdicts to inconclusive rather than silently accepting underpowered negatives.

7.5 Quality gates (all must hold for a POSITIVE verdict)
- M5 (human IAA, Fleiss' kappa) ≥ 0.60.
- M9 (adjudicator self-check accuracy) ≥ 90% per channel, where executable.
- M10 (position-swap discordance) ≤ 10%.
- Ambiguity/conflict exclusion rate on D ≤ 20% (P9).
- M4 (ChatGPT–human side concordance on non-ambiguous D) ≥ 60%; below this, the "both validators" requirement is not meaningfully satisfied.
- M6 (A-subset negative control) non-significant.

POSITIVE: all three primary tests (M1, M2a, M2b) reject in the favorable direction after Holm correction; M1b is consistent with M1; all Section 7.5 quality gates hold; both Section 7.4 power gates hold; and the M8 conservative re-analyses do not reverse the verdict.

NEGATIVE: both power gates hold; all quality gates hold; M8 does not reverse anything; but no primary test rejects in the favorable direction, and neither H2 channel shows support for the cleaned label. (A negative verdict therefore means "no evidence of higher credibility at the pre-registered power," not a proof of equivalence; this is stated in the report.)

INCONCLUSIVE: any of the following — (i) H1 and H2 point in opposite directions (e.g., cleaned model wins on gold but judges favor raw, or vice versa); (ii) any Section 7.5 quality gate fails; (iii) either Section 7.4 power gate fails; (iv) the M8 conservative re-analysis reverses a primary result; (v) M1 and M1b point in opposite directions; (vi) the P10 self-check is not executable and the channels cannot otherwise be validated.

SECTION 9 — LIMITATIONS AND UNRESOLVED UNCERTAINTIES
════════════════════════════════════════

A1 — Prediction task, features, dataset, and model architecture are unspecified in the workspace.
Why it matters: every metric, the gold construction, and the power calculations depend on them.
If violated: a regression or multiclass target changes the metrics per the Section 6 mapping (the design absorbs this via P2); a high-dimensional or weak-signal feature space changes the expected effect size and may make H1 underpowered even with real quality differences (see A8).

A2 — Docta's cleaning mechanism is unknown (rule-based vs model-based; target error classes).
Why it matters: if cleaning is stochastic or model-based, the cleaned arm is another noisy label source and H1 tests noise against noise; the credibility claim weakens to "Docta's output is at least as good."
If violated: fix the output once and freeze it (P5); interpret H1 as comparative, not absolute, credibility; M7 becomes powered per-category analysis only if the specification is confirmed.

A3 — Raw labels are assumed to be as originally collected, pre-review.
Why it matters: if raw labels already passed review, the arms differ less than assumed, D shrinks, and H2 loses power.
If violated: re-baseline the raw definition (P6); recompute the power gate; a small D may force INCONCLUSIVE by the pre-registered rule.

A4 — Human annotators are assumed competent, independent, and blind to label provenance.
Why it matters: M5 is the validity gate for the human channel; shared training bias toward Docta-style corrections (or toward original labels) would directionally bias M2b rather than measure truth.
If violated: the M5 gate or the P10 self-check should catch it; if caught, the verdict is capped at INCONCLUSIVE; if uncaught, H2-by-humans is biased in the direction of the shared bias — an irreducible risk of any human-judged design.

A5 — ChatGPT version and prompt are assumed pinnable, and ChatGPT a defensible proxy judge.
Why it matters: an unpinned version or untuned prompt makes M2a non-reproducible; LLMs have known position and phrasing biases that can systematically favor one label style.
If violated: the position-swap control (M10) and self-check (M9) are the tripwires; if either fails, the ChatGPT channel is discarded, the "both validators" requirement cannot be met, and the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE by pre-registered rule — the design fails safe rather than reporting a biased "validated by both."

A6 — "Credibility" is operationalised as predictive accuracy against adjudicated gold plus judge support on D.
Why it matters: this is the interpretive foundation (Section 2.3). It follows from the question's own terms, but it is still an interpretation.
If violated (intended meaning = label consistency/stability): the design must be restructured around test–retest metrics (repeated annotation, stability coefficients); H1/H2 as written would answer a different question. Confirm before execution.

A7 — The dataset is assumed representative and D assumed a roughly random subset of it.
Why it matters: if Docta changes labels disproportionately in a subpopulation (e.g., rare classes), the overall M2 proportion can mask subpopulation harm.
If violated: add stratified adjudication and per-stratum M2 (M7 generalizes this); the overall verdict may flip for affected strata even if the aggregate is positive.

A8 — Predictive performance against gold is assumed to be an informative proxy for label quality, and the gold itself is only as good as the adjudicators plus shared A labels.
Why it matters: a low feature ceiling (even perfect labels yield limited AUC) can make H1 undetectable despite real quality differences; noisy shared labels in A add symmetric noise to the gold.
If violated: rely more heavily on H2; report a ceiling estimate (e.g., gold-vs-gold or noise-ceiling AUC) alongside M1; the M8 gold-noise sensitivity bounds the A-label contribution.

A9 — Adjudication ambiguity is assumed rare (≤ 20% of D).
Why it matters: ambiguous items are excluded from the primary proportions; a high ambiguity rate erodes the "validated by both" claim.
If violated: the pre-registered INCONCLUSIVE criterion (Section 7.6(ii)/(iii)) triggers; the 20% threshold itself (P9) can be revisited only before execution, never after seeing results.
